articles.title: In Kyrgyzstan, public meetings with the president turn into a quest to seek justice
paragraphs: An old man in the Talas province addressing Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov during a public meeting. Photo from the Presidential Administration's website . Fair Use.

This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “ Justice as infrastructure .” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL ) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here .

In October and November 2026, Kyrgyzstan’s president, Sadyr Japarov, held public meetings with the population in all seven provinces of the country. What were meant to be formal events turned into quests for justice by people driven to desperation.
The meetings revealed the ineffectiveness of the existing justice mechanisms and showed how people saw the president as the only guarantor of justice.

The effectiveness of Kyrgyzstan’s law enforcement and judicial bodies was people’s most common justice-related complaint. During a meeting with residents of the southwestern Batken province on October 11, a woman complained to the president about her former husband, who accused her of forging their marriage certificate and framed her for crimes she did not commit to avoid the division of assets after their divorce.

She also said her former brother-in-law provided false testimony to back up his brother’s accusations. She now lives in an apartment with their three children in constant fear that her former husband may kick them out because he allegedly bribed police and courts.

This trivial legal dispute reached the point where the woman had to beg the president to ensure a just investigation and ruling. Japarov condemned her former husband and said that he should have left everything to her and their kids after the divorce.
Here is an Instagram reel with his response to the case.

On October 26, Japarov met with residents of the Kazarman district in the southern Jalalabad province, where Shirimbek Abrahmanov told the president about his father, who was imprisoned for allegedly offering a bribe of KGS 2,000 (USD 23) to a police officer during a traffic stop. The district court acquitted him of the charges.
However, the local prosecutor’s office appealed the decision in the provincial court, which found Abdrahmanov’s father guilty and sentenced him to two years in prison.
Here is an Instagram reel with the complaint and Japarov’s response.

Are the traffic police officer and the prosecutor in cahoots? Does that mean they’ve ganged up on him? If it were a large bribe, that would be one thing. But to have someone imprisoned over two thousand soms — that’s a disgrace.
The man was released from custody shortly after Japarov’s intervention and subsequent pardon.
Similar complaints resurfaced multiple times during presidential meetings in other provinces, highlighting systemic problems plaguing the judicial and law-enforcement systems.
The message is clear: people have lost all hope of finding justice at the hands of local police and courts.

Surprisingly, following his meetings with the public, Japarov concluded that the level of distrust towards courts has decreased, but admitted that problems in the judicial system remain and must be solved quickly.

On the one hand, the lack of justice and the dysfunction within the courts and police bodies, which are plagued by corruption and bureaucracy, are real pressing issues affecting millions of people across Kyrgyzstan. However, the current political regime led by Japarov, who came to power in October 2020, has made little tangible progress.
In 2026, Kyrgyzstan was ranked 99th out of 144 states in the Rule of Law Index compiled by the World Justice Project. For comparison, in 2020, it was ranked 87th .

On the other hand, people’s desperate appeals for justice helped Japarov sustain his man-of-the-people image. By listening to people’s requests and swiftly resolving their issues, the president can reinforce his popularity. In turn, this leads to the maintenance of the personalistic regime built around Japarov since his arrival to power.

articles.title: Family stories keep alive Georgia’s democratic past and the memory of Soviet repression
paragraphs: This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.

Guria is a region in Georgia, situated in the southwestern part of the country. It has a coastline on the Black Sea to the west, which is about 22 kilometers (13 miles) long, and the region is bordered by the Samegrelo-Zemo Svaneti region to the north, Imereti to the east, and the Autonomous Republic of Adjara to the south. It has a rich history and a historical tradition of democracy.
Today, in the region, independent media access is limited and digital literacy remains low. However, Guria has a civic tradition that most of its own residents do not know about in detail.

In 1904, locals organized protests against imperial (Russian, at the time) institutions, formed institutions of self-governance, and proclaimed the Gurian Republic, an early experiment in participatory democracy.

The republic was violently suppressed first by the Russian tsarist empire, and later all the memories of it were fragmented further by decades of deliberate erasure under Soviet occupation of Georgia (1921–1991) and by repressions.
This is exactly what the Digital Spark Spotlight project in Georgia focused on: history and memory in the Guria region.
Global Voices interviewed Lika Mergaladze, head of the organization Komli Initiative for Civic Engagement, about their project: what they have done and what they learned through it.
Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about yo ur organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Spark project?

Lika Mergaladze (LM) : Our organization, Komli Initiative for Civic Engagement, works to preserve local history, strengthen civic engagement, and promote sustainable development in the Guria region of Georgia. We use exhibitions, workshops, digital storytelling, and collaborative activities to connect communities with their history and encourage active participation in civic life.

We chose to get involved in the Digital Spark project because we saw an opportunity to combine local history with modern digital technologies. We wanted to help community members document and share their family stories, develop digital skills, and better understand the connection between the past and present. We believe that preserving historical memory and encouraging critical thinking are essential for building an informed and active community.
GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?

LM : One of the main challenges in Guria is that many important historical stories have been forgotten or remain untold. These stories were purposely erased during the Soviet Union. Many families who were the victims of a series of repressions in the 1920s and 30s learned to remain silent about their past in the 50s after W orld War II. As a result, younger generations often know very little about their ancestors and the region’s democratic traditions, including the Gurian Republic of 1904.

Another challenge is limited access to independent media and low levels of digital literacy in local communities. The dominance of social media and television as information sources makes media literacy and critical thinking particularly important.

We undertook this project to address these challenges by helping local people preserve their history, recognize misinformation and propaganda, and use digital tools to share their stories with a wider audience.
GV: What are the key changes/activities that your organization implemented during your participation in the project?

LM : Through the project ‘From Understanding the Past to the Digital Future,’ implemented from April to October 2026, we organized several activities across the three municipalities of Guria: Ozurgeti, Chokhatauri, and Lanchkhuti . Our main activities included a public discussion. On June 24, we organized ‘What Drove Gurians Crazy? Propaganda Now and Then,’ exploring Guria’s democratic history, Soviet occupation, propaganda, and contemporary challenges. We also did digital storytelling workshops, an AI and Digital Creation workshop and a theatrical performance: on August 12, we presented “My Days and My Father’s Diaries,” dedicated to Meri Chanukvadze and her father, Amberki Chanukvadze, whose life reflected the impact of Soviet repression. These activities helped strengthen participants’ digital skills, encourage historical research, and create opportunities for community members to share their stories online.
GV: How did your participation in the project impact your organization’s beneficiaries and the community that you serve? Please provide examples.

LM : The project generated strong interest across all three municipalities, reaching nearly 50 community members, with particularly strong participation from women and young people. Locals participated in the digital storytelling workshop, including 12 women. These activities gave participants practical opportunities to develop their digital skills and explore new ways of communicating important ideas. Another meaningful example was the theatrical performance dedicated to Meri and her father. More than 35 people attended and participated in a discussion afterwards. The performance encouraged people to reflect on the experiences of families affected by Soviet repression and the importance of preserving historical memory.

The project also laid the foundation for a cross-municipal network of young people, activists, and aspiring digital storytellers. This network can help community members continue documenting local history, sharing civic information, and engaging in public discussions beyond the project itself.
GV: How has your own knowledge, awareness, and experience with digital democracy and civic space changed, thanks to your participation in the project?

LM : Our participation in the project strengthened our understanding of how digital technologies can support civic engagement and democratic participation. We gained greater awareness of the importance of digital storytelling, media literacy, and critical thinking in helping communities understand their history and respond to contemporary challenges. We also explored how AI-assisted content creation can provide new opportunities for preserving local stories and making them accessible to wider audiences. The project reinforced our belief that digital tools are not simply communication technologies; they can also help people participate in public life, challenge misinformation, and contribute to community development. Most importantly, we recognized that connecting historical memory with modern digital tools can help create a more informed, active, and engaged society.
GV: What are the most valuable lessons and experiences you are taking away from this project?

LM : One of the most valuable lessons was that many people are interested in learning about their history when they are given a welcoming space to ask questions and share experiences. Family stories can open up broader conversations about democracy, human rights, repression, and civic responsibility.

articles.title: Companies are getting less accurate data on extreme weather just when they need it the most
paragraphs: The extreme weather fueled by an unusually intense El Niño has caused flooding in low-lying Florida communities, hammered the California coast and upended hurricane patterns – just to name a few examples.

But it also poses a growing challenge for companies that need timely climate data to manage supply chains. This information is disappearing due to federal budget cuts, leaving businesses less prepared to handle the impact of extreme weather.

To be sure, forecasters saw the 2026 El Niño coming. The Climate Prediction Center at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, or NOAA, has been forecasting a very strong El Niño since the spring, and its October update put the odds at 83% that this El Niño will become the strongest since record-keeping began in 1950, likely lasting into early 2027.
That kind of warning is valuable. It gives companies months to stock up, reroute shipments and line up backup suppliers before storms arrive or droughts set in.

But bit by bit, other valuable sources of climate data are getting cut. That includes a federal database on disasters, which adds up costs weeks after the event, that NOAA stopped updating in May 2025. The Trump administration has also cut or undercut federal climate analyses, as well as staff and funding for daily forecasting, which has left large parts of the country without coverage during extreme events – a risky prospect for businesses.

As a scholar of business operations and sustainability, I believe these cuts could have cascading effects on companies and supply chains by leaving them more vulnerable to future weather disasters. Eventually, these disruptions will hit consumers as well through higher prices.

In North America, El Niño weather patterns are linked to severe storms in the Pacific, as well as floods, fires and droughts . The economic hit can be substantial, from transportation delays to massive crop failures. Strong El Niño events have historically cost the global economy trillions of dollars .

This El Niño arrives as the pace of natural disasters picks up. While the U.S. averaged fewer than five “billion-dollar” disasters a year in the 1980s, that number now stands above 20 a year – a huge leap, even accounting for inflation. And the 2023 and 2024 totals were the highest on record.

While the scope of weather damage gets worse and worse, critical data is missing. That includes NOAA’s decision to retire its “Billion-Dollar Weather and Climate Disasters” database, ending updates after 2024.

For more than four decades, it tracked the cost of U.S. weather disasters after the fact – and businesses and researchers alike have relied on it to build prediction models. For example, scientists use these historical records to put odds on future losses or to forecast economic activity . Some of my own research also relies on historically accurate climate and weather data.
Unfortunately, the gap in climate science may be widening.

In 2025 the federal government shut down Climate.gov, which served as a central repository for weather and climate data, while its El Niño blog has been frozen since June 2025. The National Climate Assessments, the U.S. government’s preeminent reports on climate science, were taken offline, while the National Weather Service cited staff shortages as it cut back weather balloon launches at multiple sites, which feed forecast models.

Fortunately, some of these data-gathering efforts have migrated elsewhere. The scientists behind the El Niño blog have moved to a nonprofit, while another nonprofit is carrying on the efforts behind the billion-dollar disaster database.

The Trump administration has justified these cuts by citing high administrative costs and potential errors in the prediction models. But that still leaves companies, which lean on public weather data more than most shoppers realize, scrambling.

In many industries, including retail, food processing and agriculture, the payoff from acting early to safeguard supply chains can be large. Real-time and near-real-time data is used in supply chains for enhancing crop yields, finding the best routes for transport, inventory planning, and ensuring worker safety during weather emergencies. For example, Walmart invests heavily in technology and specialists to monitor weather-related disruptions and build resilient supply chains.

Another example is insurance companies, which use weather data for designing commercial insurance policies and processing claims. Risk Management Solutions Inc., a leading catastrophe risk-modeling company owned by Moody’s Corp., regularly use NOAA’s hurricane datasets to inform its advanced risk models.

When public climate data disappears, companies still need timely information to run their supply chains, so some will pay for alternative data. This typically comes from paid private services and subscriptions. Startups such as WindBorne Systems, Sofar Ocean, Tomorrow.io, Black Swift Technologies and Saildrone offer private weather balloon data and advanced climate prediction services.

While privatization can fill some gaps, it’s usually only the large retailers and insurers who can afford these forecasts. Smaller suppliers, local farmers and independent truckers further up the supply chain often can’t.
And that’s exactly where many disruptions begin.

Shoppers feel these disruptions when shortages feed into higher prices, often months later. In 2024, for example, extreme weather in the Americas, including Florida, pushed U.S. orange juice prices to an all-time high that fall. They have have stayed elevated since hurricanes Helene and Milton battered Florida’s groves.
Holiday staples are also not spared. A 2021 heat dome in the Pacific Northwest led to major damage to Christmas tree farms, causing their prices to rise an additional 5% to 10% that year .
And these effects are often global. Poor rains in West Africa more than doubled cocoa prices in 2024, and that inflation is still feeding into U.S. chocolate prices, which were up 14% in 2026 .
A historic El Niño, arriving just as federal climate data becomes sparse, makes this winter an ideal, if unfortunate, test of what climate information is really worth.

articles.title: International Court of Justice
paragraphs: The International Court of Justice (ICJ; French: Cour internationale de justice, CIJ), or colloquially the World Court, is the principal judicial organ of the United Nations (UN). It settles legal disputes submitted to it by states and provides advisory opinions on legal questions referred to it by other UN organs and specialized agencies. The ICJ is the only international court that adjudicates general disputes between countries, with its rulings and opinions serving as primary sources of international law. It is one of the six principal organs of the United Nations.

Established in June 1945 by the Charter of the United Nations, the court began work in April 1946. It is the successor to the Permanent Court of International Justice (PCIJ), which was established by the League of Nations in 1920. Its founding statute is an integral part of the UN Charter and draws heavily from that of its predecessor. All UN member states are automatically parties to the ICJ Statute, but the court's jurisdiction in contentious cases is founded upon the consent of the states party to a dispute, which may be given through special agreements or declarations accepting the court's compulsory jurisdiction.

The court comprises a panel of 15 judges elected by the UN General Assembly and Security Council to nine-year terms. The composition of the bench is required to represent the "main forms of civilization and the principal legal systems of the world", and no two judges may be nationals of the same country. The ICJ is seated in the Peace Palace in The Hague, Netherlands, making it the only principal UN organ not in New York City. Its official working languages are English and French.

Since its first case was submitted in 1947, the court has entertained 201 cases as of September 2025. While its judgments are binding on the parties and final, the ICJ has no formal enforcement mechanism. Enforcement of its rulings is ultimately a political matter for the UN Security Council, where it is subject to the veto power of the five permanent members.

The first permanent institution established for the purpose of settling international disputes was the Permanent Court of Arbitration (PCA), which was created by the Hague Peace Conference of 1899. Initiated by the Russian Tsar Nicholas II, the conference involved all the world's major powers, as well as several smaller states, and resulted in the first multilateral treaties concerned with the conduct of warfare. Among these was the Convention for the Pacific Settlement of International Disputes, which set forth the institutional and procedural framework for arbitral proceedings, which would take place in The Hague, Netherlands. Although the proceedings would be supported by a permanent bureau—whose functions would be equivalent to that of a secretariat or court registry—the arbitrators would be appointed by the disputing states from a larger pool provided by each member of the convention. The PCA was established in 1900 and began proceedings in 1902.

A second Hague Peace Conference in 1907, which involved most of the world's sovereign states, revised the convention and enhanced the rules governing arbitral proceedings before the PCA. During this conference, the United States, Great Britain and Germany submitted a joint proposal for a permanent court whose judges would serve full-time. As the delegates could not agree how the judges would be selected, the matter was shelved pending an agreement to be adopted at a later convention.

The Hague Peace Conferences, and the ideas that emerged therefrom, influenced the creation of the Central American Court of Justice, which was established in 1908 as one of the earliest regional judicial bodies. Various plans and proposals were made between 1911 and 1919 for the establishment of an international judicial tribunal, which would not be realized in the formation of a new international system after World War I.

The unprecedented bloodshed of the First World War led to the creation of the League of Nations, established by the Paris Peace Conference of 1919 as the first worldwide intergovernmental organization aimed at maintaining peace and collective security. Article 14 of the League of Nations Covenant called for the establishment of a Permanent Court of International Justice (PCIJ), which would be responsible for adjudicating any international dispute submitted to it by the contesting parties, and provide advisory opinions upon any disputes or questions referred to it by the League of Nations.

In December 1920, after several drafts and debates, the Assembly of the league unanimously adopted the statute of the PCIJ, which was signed and ratified in 1921 by a majority of members. Among other things, the new statute resolved the contentious issues of selecting judges by providing that the judges be elected by both the council and the Assembly of the league concurrently but independently. The makeup of the PCIJ would reflect the "main forms of civilization and the principal legal systems of the world". The PCIJ would be permanently placed at the Peace Palace in The Hague, alongside the Permanent Court of Arbitration.

Unlike the ICJ, the PCIJ was not part of the league, nor were members of the league automatically a party to its statute. The United States, which played a key role in both the second Hague Peace Conference and the Paris Peace Conference, was notably not a member of the league, but several of its nationals served as judges of the court.

From its first session in 1922 until 1940, the PCIJ dealt with 29 interstate disputes and issued 27 advisory opinions. Several hundred international treaties and agreements conferred jurisdiction upon the court over specified categories of disputes, reflecting the court's widespread acceptance. In addition to helping resolve several serious international disputes, the PCIJ helped clarify several ambiguities in international law that contributed to its development.

The United States played a major role in setting up the PCIJ but never joined. Presidents Woodrow Wilson, Warren G. Harding, Calvin Coolidge, Herbert Hoover and Franklin D. Roosevelt all supported membership, but did not get the two-thirds majority in the Senate required for a treaty.
The court deal only with judicial, not political matters.

Several months later at the Moscow conference in 1943, the major Allies—China, the USSR, the U.K., and the U.S.—issued a joint declaration recognizing the necessity "of establishing at the earliest practicable date a general international organization, based on the principle of the sovereign equality of all peace-loving States, and open to membership by all such States, large and small, for the maintenance of international peace and security".

articles.title: Avoiding the ‘F word’: Australia and Turkey dance around fossil fuels at COP31 summit
paragraphs: One phrase has been glaringly absent from this year’s COP31 climate summit .

Fossil fuels are not mentioned in the COP31 priority areas . Key speeches from the leaders of Australia and Turkey (Türkiye), co-hosts of the conference, have largely failed to address the emissions-shaped elephant in the room.
That’s despite mounting pressure from environmental groups, Pacific nations and COP30 host nation Brazil to abandon coal, oil and gas and slash global emissions.
So why does this matter? And what does it mean for climate action worldwide?
In their opening speeches, neither Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan nor Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese mentioned fossil fuels.

At the official commencement of COP31, the Australian president of negotiations and environment minister, Chris Bowen, twice uttered the words fossil fuels. Neither reference was tied to specific goals for a global fossil fuel phase out or weaning Australia, one of the world’s largest exporters of coal and gas, off them. In his opening remarks, Turkey’s environment minister Murat Kurum didn’t mention them at all.
This reluctance to spotlight fossil fuels is also reflected in the priority areas, or main aims, of COP31 that were agreed by the co-host nations.

The headline goal is the “ 35-by-35 ” target to produce 35% of the world’s energy from electricity, increasingly using renewables, by 2035. Other priorities include halving the growth of global waste and cutting energy consumption in the building sector .
Yet, nowhere in sight is a plan or timeline to eliminate fossil fuels.

Negotiators may point to previous COPs, where the very mention of fossil fuels has sparked contention. At COP30 in Brazil, major oil producers Russia and Saudi Arabia fought hard to ensure fossil fuels did not feature in the final agreed text. In comparison, the 2035 electrification goal may be more likely to achieve consensus .

But there’s a simpler explanation for this fossil fuel avoidance: any discussion of these fuels would undermine the credibility of the co-host nations as climate leaders, given their common reliance on coal, oil and gas.

Australia is the world’s third-largest exporter of fossil fuels, behind only Russia and the United States. These offshore emissions bring Australia’s total emissions close to 5% of the global footprint. What’s more, Australia continued approving new fossil fuel mining projects, even after its role at COP31 was confirmed.

Turkey is not a fossil fuel exporter but remains a major consumer of them, particularly coal . On the eve of COP31 talks, Turkish President Erdogan was criticised for celebrating the discovery of two significant new oil fields.
Abandoning fossil fuels clearly isn’t a priority of this year’s hosting team. But this doesn’t necessarily extend to other nations attending COP31.

In the lead-up to COP31, civil society and environmental groups, including Greenpeace and Amnesty, voiced their disappointment that fossil fuels were largely left out of the official agenda. While recognising the headline goals as worthy aims, some organisations criticised the agenda as being not ambitious enough, given the scale of the climate crisis.

Pacific countries have also pushed hard for an end to fossil fuels, notably through a fossil fuel treaty that would establish concrete plans and timelines. These small island nations have also declared Australia’s approval of new fossil fuel projects as “ immoral and unacceptable ”. This criticism is particularly telling, given Australia made its co-hosting bid with the aim of spotlighting the climate vulnerability of its Pacific neighbours .

Brazil has also emerged as a vocal critic of this year’s co-hosts. After leading the preceding COP30 conference, Brazil formally presented its global roadmap for transitioning away from fossil fuels to several high-profile UN leaders, making a splash on the second day of COP31 negotiations. The roadmap is a practical guide offering targets, timetables and other considerations to help countries shift away from fossil fuels. After speaking to the challenge of climate change, newly re-elected President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva urged his COP31 audience to turn the roadmap into concrete action.
This debate over whether to call out the world’s reliance on fossil fuels is problematic, not least because it points to a failure of global climate cooperation.

The science is clear: greenhouse gas emissions from coal, oil and gas are driving climate change . With the world on track to “ overshoot ” the Paris Agreement target of 1.5°C, reducing and ultimately eliminating fossil fuel use must be a priority.
But there is still hope. While fossil fuels may be a source of discomfort for Australia and Turkey, this debate could spur global climate action in other ways.

Introducing the global roadmap, for instance, could make the comparatively modest 35-by-35 electrification goal more appealing, particularly to countries that remain reluctant to phase out fossil fuels. This “decarbonisation by stealth” approach could help lower global emissions. However, some nations may support the electrification goal but still resist calls to get that electricity from renewables. In that sense, failing to directly target fossil fuels may lead to partial or imperfect climate action.

Nevertheless, expect the “F word” – fossil fuels – to remain centre stage during the second week of COP31 and future climate summits. We simply can’t afford to keep kicking this dirty can down the road.

articles.title: European Space Agency
paragraphs: The European Space Agency is a 23-member international organisation devoted to space exploration. It has its headquarters in Paris and a staff of around 3,000 people globally as of 2025. ESA was founded in 1975 in the context of European integration. Its 2026 annual budget was around €8.3 billion.

The ESA human spaceflight programme includes participation in the International Space Station (ISS) and collaboration with NASA on the Artemis programme, especially manufacturing of the Orion spacecraft's European Service Module (ESM). ESA launches and operates uncrewed missions to the Moon, Mars, Jupiter, Venus, Mercury, the Sun, and various comets and asteroids. Other activities include space telescopes, Earth observation satellites, asteroid impact avoidance, telecommunication and navigation satellites, designing launch vehicles (e.g. Ariane 6 is operated through Arianespace with ESA sharing in the costs), and maintaining Europe's spaceport (the Guiana Space Centre in Kourou, French Guiana), as well as space safety and commercialisation.

"The purpose of the Agency shall be to provide for and to promote, for exclusively peaceful purposes, cooperation among European States in space research and technology and their space applications, with a view to their being used for scientific purposes and for operational space applications systems."

ESA is responsible for setting a unified space and related industrial policy, recommending space objectives to the member states, and integrating national programmes like satellite development, into the European programme as much as possible.

"Today space activities have pursued the benefit of citizens, and citizens are asking for a better quality of life on Earth. They want greater security and economic wealth, but they also want to pursue their dreams, to increase their knowledge, and they want younger people to be attracted to the pursuit of science and technology.
"ESA's intergovernmental framework provides the credentials and tools for developing space technologies and systems [...] for security and defence and to implement corresponding activities."

After World War II, many European scientists left Western Europe to work with the United States. Although the 1950s boom made it possible for Western European countries to invest in research and specifically in space-related activities, Western European scientists realised solely national projects would not be able to compete with the two superpowers. In 1958, only months after the Sputnik shock, Edoardo Amaldi (Italy) and Pierre Auger (France), two prominent members of the Western European scientific community, met to discuss the foundation of a common Western European space agency. The meeting was attended by scientific representatives from eight countries.

The Western European nations decided to have two agencies: one concerned with developing a launch system, ELDO (European Launcher Development Organisation), of which Renzo Carrobio di Carrobio became the first Secretary General from 1964 to 1971, and the other the precursor of the European Space Agency, ESRO (European Space Research Organisation), led by Pierre Auger. The latter was established on 20 March 1964 by an agreement signed on 14 June 1962. From 1968 to 1972, ESRO launched seven research satellites, but ELDO was not able to deliver a launch vehicle. Both agencies struggled with the underfunding and diverging interests of their participants.

The ESA in its current form was founded with the ESA Convention in 1975, when ESRO was merged with ELDO. ESA had ten founding member states: Belgium, Denmark, France, West Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, and the United Kingdom. These signed the ESA Convention in 1975 and deposited the instruments of ratification by 1980, when the convention came into force. During this interval the agency functioned in a de facto fashion.

ESA launched its first major scientific mission in 1975, Cos-B, a satellite monitoring gamma-ray emissions in the universe, which was first worked on by ESRO. ESA collaborated with NASA on the International Ultraviolet Explorer (IUE), the world's first high-orbit telescope, which was launched in 1978 and operated successfully for 18 years. A number of successful Earth-orbit projects followed, and in 1986 ESA began Giotto, its first deep-space mission, to study the comets Halley and Grigg–Skjellerup. Hipparcos, a star-mapping mission, was launched in 1989 and in the 1990s SOHO, Ulysses, and the Hubble Space Telescope were all jointly carried out with NASA. Later scientific missions in cooperation with NASA include the Cassini–Huygens space probe, to which the ESA contributed by building the Titan landing module Huygens.

As the successor of ELDO, the ESA has also constructed rockets for scientific and commercial payloads. Ariane 1, launched in 1979, carried mostly commercial payloads into orbit from 1984 onward. The next two versions of the Ariane rocket family were intermediate stages in the development of a more advanced launch system, the Ariane 4, which operated between 1988 and 2003 and established the ESA as the world leader in commercial space launches in the 1990s. Although the succeeding Ariane 5 experienced a failure on its first flight in 1996, it has since firmly established itself within the heavily competitive commercial space launch market with 112 successful launches until 2023. In 1998, ESA started developing the small-lift launch vehicle Vega.

Astronauts from the future ESA member states have been joining Soviet space missions since 1978. The first ESA astronaut to fly to space was Ulf Merbold who joined the STS-9 mission of the American Space Shuttle in 1983, that carried the first European-built Spacelab laboratory module. The experience gained during the Spacelab programme was later instrumental in developing the International Space Station (ISS). Since then, ESA astronauts have been joining Space Shuttle flights, as well as Russian Soyuz flights to the Mir space station. During the 1980s and 1990s, ESA was considering developing its own crewed spacecraft Hermes and a small space station Columbus MTFF. These plans were later abandoned and instead, ESA joined the ISS programme with Columbus being repurposed as one of the station's laboratory modules and ESA astronauts flying to the station on American and Russian spacecraft.

The beginning of the new millennium saw the ESA become, along with agencies like NASA and JAXA, one of the major participants in space research. articles.title: Why does your body store fat in your butt?
paragraphs: Curious Kids is a series for children of all ages. If you have a question you’d like an expert to answer, send it to CuriousKidsUS@theconversation.com .
Have you ever wondered why some parts of your body are firm, like your elbows, while other areas, like your butt, are squishier?
The difference is due to what scientists call fat distribution, and researchers are still trying to understand why bodies store fat in some places but not in others.
All animals have fat in their bodies, even insects . Bears even put on up to 400 pounds (180 kilograms) of additional body fat, the equivalent of 544 large cheese pizzas, to survive hibernation .
Fat is an important and constantly changing part of all bodies, including those of humans and our evolutionary ancestors.
Fat, also called adipose tissue, is one kind of connective tissue that helps hold your body together.

For a long time, scientists thought that adipose tissue was mainly a storage place for the extra energy your body doesn’t use from the food you eat. While fat is a great source of stored energy, it also has many other functions. There are even different kinds of fat.

Visceral fat serves as a sort of protective bubble wrap, surrounding and filling in the spaces between your internal organs. Subcutaneous fat, the layer of fat between your skin and your muscle that you can pinch, is a protective cushion and helps to keep you warm by insulating you like a coat.
Fat also produces and responds to hormones, a type of chemical messenger, to regulate how your body uses energy and to tell you when you are hungry or full.
Different kinds of fat also have different jobs. White fat is the kind of fat most people are familiar with and performs the functions mentioned above.
You may be less familiar with brown fat, which is brown because it contains a lot of mitochondria : the parts of your cells that produce the energy your body needs to perform all its functions.

Not all animals have brown fat, but humans do. Scientists know that brown fat performs a special function to heat your body when you get cold. It doesn’t store energy, like white fat does, to help your body move.

When you were a baby, you had a lot of brown fat along your torso to help keep you warm because your body wasn’t mature enough to maintain your body temperature. As you grow older, you have less brown fat . It is only located just above your collar bone and along your major deep blood vessels, like your aorta .

Researchers don’t know enough yet about brown fat to know why it is in just a few parts of the body. It is possible that it’s near the neck and around major blood vessels to help insulate the blood and keep overall body temperature in a healthy warm range.
As for white fat, there appear to be three main factors that determine where your fat gets stored: genetics, hormones and age.
Certain genes direct fat to accumulate in the butt, while other genes tell it to collect on the torso.

Hormones like estrogen, which affects almost every system in all bodies but is typically higher in females, direct more subcutaneous fat to gather in the butt, thighs and backs of the arms. Cortisol, the stress hormone, seems to direct visceral fat to accumulate in the belly area.

But why isn’t fat evenly distributed throughout the body? Well, having a lot of fat around your elbows and knees would limit your ability to bend your arms and legs. Storing a lot of fat around your head would possibly put your brain at risk of overheating . Other parts of your body, like hips, butts, breasts and thighs, don’t have these risks – maybe that’s why we store fat there.

Don’t be fooled: A lot of animals that look fat, like a hippopotamus, actually aren’t. Hippos only have around 2% body fat, the percentage of how much of your body mass comes from fat; while the average human woman has over 30% body fat .

In the rest of the animal kingdom, biologists typically only see a lot of body fat among hibernating or marine mammals . For the hibernators, the fat serves as energy storage for long, cold winters. For marine mammals like seals and whales, that extra fat is like a giant puffy coat helping to keep them warm in the cold depths of the ocean.
Humans do not hibernate, nor do we live in the ocean, so why do we have a lot more fat than all other primates and most mammals?

Anthropologists like me, who study how the human body has evolved over time, think it has to do with the lifestyle of our evolutionary ancestors who had to gather and hunt to survive. Gathering and hunting were not always reliable food sources . We think our ancestors developed the ability to put on extra fat as a food insurance policy. When food was difficult to find, they could rely on their extra fat stores to carry them through until food became available again.
Researchers are still trying to determine when this extra fat storage evolved. We have one line of evidence from small stone figures known as Gravettian statues .
These ancient statues from 25,000 to 28,000 years ago depict feminine figures who carry a lot of extra body fat. Archaeologists have found them all throughout Europe and Russia.

The way the ancient artists depicted fat on these figures matches how fat looks on bodies today. This accuracy has led researchers to believe that the makers of the Gravettian statues knew how individuals with greater body fat actually looked, meaning at least some people at this time did put on a lot of extra fat.

Europe and Russia back then were much colder than they are today, supporting the idea that our ancestors would have needed the extra fat to get through the extremely cold winters when food was harder to find.
So, the next time you poke at your butt fat, remember that fat is a really important part of our bodies, performs lots of different functions, and is likely evolutionarily ancient for us humans.

articles.title: From solving to ‘digesting’: How mathematicians can adapt to the dramatic changes AI has brought to their field
paragraphs: On Nov. 20, 2026, a mathematician at the AI company Anthropic claimed that while working with the model Claude, he had solved the generalized Riemann hypothesis, the most famous problem in mathematics. This problem has stood unsolved for 167 years, and solving it could easily warrant a Fields Medal – considered equivalent to a Nobel Prize, but for mathematics. In its current state, however, the solution is roughly 250,000 pages long, so it will take a while before human mathematicians can be satisfied that it is correct.

This proof emerged a month after OpenAI released 722 mathematics research papers that contained results generated by an internal AI model. While they have already retracted some of the papers due to mistakes, others, assuming they are correct, would also be impressive enough to earn a Fields Medal.

If AI can generate papers that would take a human mathematician years to research and write, does that mean mathematics is dead? Many headlines have been asking this question – and some school-age children may be rejoicing.

But it’s not that simple. I’ve been a mathematician for 45 years, and my work has taught me that mathematics is not just about solving problems or proving theorems. It is about understanding why the solutions and proofs work and then extending that mathematics to new contexts.

Fueling this existential crisis is the fact that over the past century, mathematicians have come to attach greater prestige to the solution and the proof than the understanding. Now that an AI can come up with a solution and a proof, the underlying understanding could vanish. Mathematicians are being forced to rethink what they value.
If you’re not a mathematician, this crisis might seem inconsequential. But math isn’t all abstract problems. It’s used to design and optimize technology that’s essential to modern society.

One example is MRI, or magnetic resonance imaging . MRI is a very useful tool in medical diagnosis. X-rays see only your bones, but MRI machines allow a physician to see the soft tissue inside a person in a noninvasive manner.

MRI scans used to require a patient to lie still inside a metal tube for up to half an hour or more while a loud machine made images by scanning back and forth. At the end, it combined the images. This process was difficult for many adults and virtually impossible for children without sedation.

Modern MRI machines require many fewer scans in a shorter period, and they get better resolution. Now, more patients find the procedure no big deal. The key to this vast improvement was the mathematics of compressed sensing, a relatively recent invention.

Compressed sensing allows the machine to construct an image from fewer scans. At first, doing so didn’t seem possible. But in the mid 2000s, a mathematician, statisticians and an electrical engineer figured out how to use the fact that many of the scans are very similar to develop the mathematics that made compressed sensing possible.

They showed that images can be reconstructed from far fewer samples than previously thought necessary. This solution required a deep understanding of many different areas of mathematics, and even the development of new mathematics. Moreover, it involved asking the right questions – something I believe current AI models would not have known how to do.

Today’s iterations of AI may have been able to speed up the invention of compressed sensing, with humans in the loop. But coming up with the mathematics behind compressed sensing most likely would have been beyond the current capabilities of AI by itself.

AI-led research still requires the involvement of human mathematicians. But mathematicians are now asking each other what they have to change about their approach and the field’s norms. Many problems that would have been given to Ph.D. students to solve for their dissertation can now be done by AI.

But most of Open AI’s 722 mathematics research papers are not understandable to a human mathematician, and this is certainly the case for the claimed proof of the generalized Riemann hypothesis. Even the outputs from these papers that have gone through the proof-checking software Lean, which can verify a proof, are often incomprehensible to a human. AI’s current mathematical writing ability is quite primitive.

In other words, the mathematics will be known to be true by the mathematicians, but they won’t have a clue in most cases as to why it is true. And if there is no understanding as to why, then the mathematics loses its value. If you don’t know why it works, then you can’t apply the math.

As Terrence Tao, the mathematician who solved the MRI problem, has said, mathematicians will now have to place value on the digestion of the proofs . By digestion he means absorbing, simplifying and contextualizing the proof.

Once digested, researchers gain understanding, and then the ability to apply the results in new realms. Many mathematicians are now arguing that Ph.D. programs should change their emphasis from solving a problem to solving, digesting and then showing understanding by explaining the solution to other mathematicians and colleagues in other scientific fields.

Mathematicians will also have to change how they teach their classes. AI can now easily solve any standard math homework problem. To get around this, instructors might try to design their classes around understanding, rather than reaching solutions. They might accomplish this shift using oral exams or class presentations.

Many mathematicians – me included – view this shift in the field as an opportunity to emphasize understanding. The invention of the calculator freed students from computation. AI may do the same at another level.

AI is not just changing mathematics. It will affect other disciplines, too. It is already speeding up the development of new materials and chemicals. In these fields, human scientists will still want to verify that the model yields what they desire.

Four years ago, ChatGPT was incapable of basic arithmetic. These models have progressed very quickly, so it’s hard to say where mathematics will be in the future. But regardless, learning math teaches students important problem-solving and critical-thinking skills that AI cannot, at least at this point in time, entirely replace.
David Manderscheid is on the National Academy of Sciences Board of Mathematical Sciences and Analytics and the Board of Trustees of the Institute for Pure and Applied Mathematics.

articles.title: What are AI chips, and what’s so special about Nvidia’s?
paragraphs: The commotion around Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s ouster and reinstatement, the central role of Nvidia in the U.S.-China AI competition, and the U.S. economy’s reliance on the AI boom might leave you asking: What’s so special about Nvidia’s chips?
The answer comes down to graphics processing units, or GPUs, and how far they’ve come from their humble beginnings as sidekicks to computers’ main chips: central processing units, or CPUs.
GPUs now power the most visible advances in generative artificial intelligence, but they began as modestly priced add-on cards for video games and video rendering.

As a researcher of high-performance computing and computer processors, I see three factors that explain how GPUs have become so important to the modern economy and how Nvidia became their dominant supplier: software that made GPUs useful beyond graphics, a research breakthrough that showed what they could do for AI, and a global commercial and political race to build ever-larger AI models.

The CPU is built to handle a wide variety of complicated tasks quickly, a few at a time. In contrast, a GPU typically operates on simpler mathematical tasks, such as multiplying two sets of numbers, but it can perform many of these simpler operations in parallel.

A GPU’s design turns out to be ideal for AI. Training a neural network, the kind of AI model behind today’s chatbots and image generators, comes down mostly to multiplying enormous grids of numbers, over and over. Today’s top AI GPUs can perform more than a quadrillion, or thousand trillion, of these operations every second.

Early GPUs could only draw graphics. Programmers controlled them with small programs called shaders, which calculate things such as the color of each pixel and which can be repeated across millions of pixels in parallel. Nvidia dominated the market for graphics chips in the late 1990s and 2000s.

In the early 2000s, Stanford University researchers built software tools that let programmers use this hardware for other kinds of calculations. That work provided the basis for Nvidia’s Compute Unified Device Architecture, or CUDA, which was released in 2007. CUDA allowed scientists and engineers to run scientific and more general purpose programs using the GPU’s parallel execution model.

The second major shift occurred when AlexNet, a neural network model developed and trained on GPUs, won the 2012 ImageNet challenge, an annual competition to see which software could most accurately identify objects in a set of photographs. AlexNet was trained on two Nvidia GPUs, and it made far fewer mistakes than any competitor. The result showed that GPUs made it practical to train neural networks big enough to beat the older techniques, and AI researchers quickly adopted them for their work.

Because Nvidia had spent years building CUDA and the software around it, it was positioned to benefit more than anyone. Competitors, including AMD, which also makes GPUs, and Google, which designs its own AI chips, called tensor processing units, have since built strong alternatives.

Nvidia and other chipmakers then began redesigning GPUs for AI with specific features. These include adding hardware specialized for the matrix multiplication math that neural networks rely on, using reduced precision numbers to improve the speed of neural network training and adding larger amounts of fast memory to keep these chips supplied with data for AI workloads.

In 2017, Google researchers introduced the transformer, a neural network design originally built to translate between languages. Transformers turned out to perform remarkably well in terms of accuracy as the model and dataset size grew, and this design became the foundation of today’s chatbots and many other generative AI systems.

The growth of these new transformer models has also led to the current boom of generative AI companies, including U.S.-based companies OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Google and xAI, as well as Chinese companies such as DeepSeek, Alibaba and Baidu. Each of these companies is actively focused on building large data centers composed of high-end GPUs to train next-generation foundation models.

These foundation models, exemplified by Google’s Gemini, Anthropic’s Claude Fable and OpenAI’s GPT Astra, are very large neural networks that can reason, write software code and analyze information in response to plain language instructions. The companies working on foundation model training are betting that the best models will automate much of the world’s information work and generate enormous economic returns.

Nvidia trains some AI models of its own, but most of its profit comes from selling the chips and software that other companies use to build theirs. This AI boom has led to record profits for Nvidia, but it has also drawn attention from the U.S. government, which has debated how far to restrict sales of advanced chips to China. The Trump administration tightened its export controls for advanced GPUs in the immediate aftermath of the scandal involving Huang’s relationship with an alleged Chinese spy .

Demand for AI chips looks likely to keep growing as the leading AI companies compete to build more capable models, but the boom faces real limits. AI data centers require enormous amounts of electricity, raising questions about the power costs and environmental impacts to local communities.

The most advanced AI chips, including Nvidia’s, are fabricated largely by one company, Taiwanese chip giant Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., known as TSMC. Demand for AI hardware has also strained supplies of memory chips, creating shortages that reach gaming graphics cards and smartphones.

Nvidia also faces direct competition from AMD, cloud companies designing their own chips, and startups, all promising to run AI more cheaply and with less power. Whether Nvidia’s software and hardware advantages can hold off these challengers is one of the biggest open questions in the industry.
Jeffrey Young has received donations from NVIDIA academic hardware grant programs in the past and has coauthored academic publications with current and former NVIDIA employees.

articles.title: NASA Navigation Experiment Shows Promise for Planetary Landings
paragraphs: Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater)
NASA successfully demonstrated technology designed to help spacecraft autonomously navigate to safe landing sites on the Moon and on other planets.

An Alta-X drone equipped with the agency’s Safe and Precise Landing – Integrated Capabilities Evolution (SPLICE ) guidance, navigation, and control payload completed simulated lunar descent and landing maneuvers Aug. 27. The flight took place at Rogers Dry Lake near NASA’s Armstrong Flight Research Center in Edwards, California.

During the tests, the SPLICE payload used an advanced guidance system to map the terrain and assess potential landing areas. If the system determines the targeted landing area is unsafe, the system diverts the drone to a safer location. The system generates high-resolution digital elevation maps from light-detection and sensor data.

Researchers at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston developed the SPLICE payload and partnered with specialists at NASA Armstrong to integrate, test, and fly it aboard the Alta-X drone in June and July. Those tests verified communications, data handling, telemetry, and command- control performance between the SPLICE payload and the drone to prepare for a full-scale test at Voyager Technologies in Mojave, California, later this month.

“This flight test is the culmination of almost a decade of work, for the SPLICE project,” said Davis Adams, NASA project manager. “This flight raised the technology readiness level, priming it for integration into future robotic and crewed lunar flights. Validation of the guidance and navigation systems are applicable to terrestrial, lunar, and Martian descent and landing missions.”

NASA has worked with a number of commercial lunar lander providers to implement iterations of SPLICE into their platforms. A number of the landers slated for upcoming Moon Base missions leverage data collected by NASA through the development of systems like SPLICE to execute soft touchdowns on the lunar surface.

“We are coordinating with industry regarding the usage of the guidance system once the system is available in the NASA software catalog, currently planned for this fall,” Adams said. “Some of the companies also are evaluating the system’s navigation capabilities for precision landing applications, as well as potential extensions for autonomous surface mobility.”

NASA’s Flight Opportunities project, based at NASA Armstrong, enabled flight testing of the SPLICE project early in its development that laid a foundation for it to continue advancing its technology readiness level to what it is today. Flight testing included both a descent altitude and a landing trajectory in 2019 similar to what is expected on a lunar mission and the demonstration of two NASA-developed precision landing sensor systems in 2020.

articles.title: Infancy Gospel of Thomas
paragraphs: The Infancy Gospel of Thomas (also known as the Infancy of Jesus or Childhood of Jesus, the Paidika tou Iesou or Paidika (Greek), and abbreviated as Inf. Gos. Thom. or IGT) is an apocryphal gospel about the childhood of Jesus. Together with the Gospel of James, it was one of the earliest and most influential sources detailing the activities and life of the young Jesus, although neither are included in the New Testament canon. Its creation is generally dated to the second century. The oldest extant fragmentary writing is in Koine Greek and dates to the fourth or fifth century; Latin and Syriac attestations to a short form exist from the fifth or sixth century; and an 11th-century manuscript in Greek (Codex Sabaiticus) contains the earliest extant long form of the work. Variants flourished that expanded the infancy gospel by combining it with other stories in larger works and anthologies; the Gospel of Pseudo-Matthew is one example that proved popular in the Latin-speaking Western Church during the Middle Ages.

The Infancy Gospel of Thomas depicts a young Jesus in full possession of divine power and already dispensing wisdom with authority, even at an early age. It includes several miracles that spread widely and appear in other sources, such as Jesus's transforming clay sparrows into live sparrows. Jesus sometimes wields his power in a capricious way, such as when he curses and kills those who cross him. Although the Jesus depicted in this gospel can be an "enfant terrible", he balances this with miracles and healing.

The author of the work is not known. Some versions include a pseudepigraphal attribution to "Thomas the Israelite", which might be a reference to Thomas the Apostle, but this attribution appears to date to the medieval period and is only in some manuscripts. The work varies greatly in style from the canonical gospels. The Infancy Gospel of Thomas ends with its account of Jesus in the temple at age 12, a story originally from the Gospel of Luke.

During the era of early Christianity, many stories of Jesus of Nazareth circulated among Christians eager to hear details of his life, usually called gospels. Most scholars suggest that the earliest form of the collection of stories that would eventually be titled the Infancy Gospel of Thomas dates to the mid-to-late second century. Versions of the work and the stories within it appear to have been popular, with a wide geographical spread and many translations to different languages. The earliest forms of the work may have spread via oral tradition, either wholly or as several different stories.

Eventually it was transcribed to writing, and over time redacted and adapted. The earliest evidence of the text comes from the late second century. Two 2nd-century documents, the Epistle of the Apostles (by an unknown author) and Against Heresies (by Irenaeus), refer to a story of Jesus's tutor telling him, "Say alpha", and Jesus replying, "First tell me what is beta, and I can tell you what alpha is". Irenaeus, whose work is dated to around 180 AD, did not give a name to the book he quoted from; he condemned this book as spurious and heretical. Irenaeus's reference suggests that an early form of the infancy gospel circulating in the 2nd century would be plausible. There are further references that seem to indicate the spread of the stories; the Syriac form of the third-century Acts of Thomas contains a possible mention. In the fourth century, Epiphanius of Salamis's Panarion quotes Jesus's childhood miracles approvingly, but John Chrysostom condemns these stories of childhood miracles as false.

The author or authors of the gospel are unknown. The author was probably a gentile Christian, as the work displays no knowledge of Judaism. The author was educated and knew some rare words in an era when literacy was uncommon, but wrote in a style that was overall simple and readable. The geographic origin of the author is also unknown, leaving scholars with little more than guesses. Jan Bremmer suggests Alexandria in Roman Egypt as plausible. Tony Burke suggests it was a place where the Gospel of Luke was held in high regard: perhaps Asia Minor (modern Turkey) or Antioch in Roman Syria. Others such as Sever Voicu have suggested Roman Palestine. J.R.C. Cousland cautions that the safest, if least specific, suggestion is somewhere in the Greek-speaking Eastern Roman Empire.

The early versions of the work are anonymous. No author is indicated in the earliest surviving manuscripts (Latin, Syriac, Georgian, Ethiopic). In some later manuscripts dating from the Middle Ages, the gospel opens with a prologue where "Thomas the Israelite" introduces himself as the author, but with no further explanation. It is possible that this was meant to hint that the author was Judas Thomas, known as Thomas the Apostle, thought by some Christians to be a brother of Jesus and thus familiar with young Jesus's activities. Some medieval Latin versions close with an epilogue where the author claims to have been an eyewitness who witnessed these events personally, another claim that seems to have been added centuries after the original story's circulation. Two other figures have been attributed claims of authorship: John the Evangelist in some early Latin translations, and James, brother of Jesus in some Greek versions.

The text describes the life of the child Jesus from the ages of five to twelve, with fanciful, and sometimes malevolent, supernatural events. He is presented as a precocious child who starts his education early. This summary uses the order in the Greek A recension, one of the versions that has received the most attention and analysis.

A five-year old Jesus is playing in the mud after rain near a river. He organizes the water into pools. With a single word, he miraculously cleanses the water. He then crafts 12 sparrows from the clay while playing with other children. A Jew, displeased with seeing children work on the Sabbath, reports this to Jesus's father Joseph. Jesus gives life to the sparrows and they fly off. Another boy, the son of Annas, breaks the pools Jesus made, letting their water drain out. Jesus pronounces a curse upon the boy, and he instantly withers. The parents ineffectively complain to Joseph.

Later, another child either bumps into Jesus while running, throws a stone, or punches him (depending on the manuscript). Jesus kills the other boy by pronouncing a curse on him. The parents of the dead child complain to Joseph, and he rebukes Jesus. Jesus curses his accusers with blindness. Joseph then pulls his ear.

articles.title: Treaty of Granada (1491)
paragraphs: The Treaty of Granada, also known as the Surrender of Granada or the Capitulations, was signed and ratified on November 25, 1491, between Boabdil, the sultan of Granada, and Ferdinand and Isabella, the King and Queen of Castile, León, Aragon, and Sicily. It ended the Granada War, which had started in 1482 and culminated in the siege and battle of Granada, which began in spring 1491.

The Treaty of Granada was not merely a military surrender but the result of a decade of attrition known as the Granada War (1482-1492). The Nasrid Kingdom, the last vestige of Al-Andalus, was crippled by internal civil war between Sultan Boabdil (Muhammad XII) and his father and uncle.

Ferdinand and Isabella exploited this instability, capturing key cities like Malaga and Baza. By the time the siege of Granada began in the spring of 1491, the city was overcrowded with refugees and facing starvation. The treaty was negotiated in secret over several months to prevent a riot among the city's populace who were not yet ready to concede.

The Capitulations of Granada established a comprehensive set of conditions intended to ensure a peaceful transition of power while safeguarding the legal, religious, and social rights of the Muslim inhabitants.
That their mosques and the religious endowments appertaining to them should remain as they were in the times of Islam.
That the Christians who had embraced Islam should not be compelled to relinquish it and adopt their former creed.

That any Muslim wishing to become a Christian should be allowed some days to consider the step he was about to take, after which he was to be questioned by both a Muslim and a Christian judge concerning his intended change and if, after that examination, he still refused to return to Islam, he should be permitted to follow his own inclination.

That no muezzin should be interrupted in the act of calling the people to prayer and no Muslim molested either in the performance of his daily devotions or in the observance of his fast or in any other religious ceremony, but if a Christian should be found laughing at them, he should be punished for it.
That the Muslims should be exempted from all taxation for a certain number of years.
That no increase should be made to the usual imposts but that on the contrary all oppressive taxes lately imposed should be immediately suppressed.
That their laws should be preserved as they were before and that no one should judge them except by those same laws.
That no Christian or Jew holding public offices by the appointment of the late Sultan should be allowed to exercise his functions or rule over them.
That no one should be prosecuted and punished for the crime of another man.
That no Muslim should be prosecuted for the death of a Christian slain during the siege and that no restitution of property taken during the war should be enforced.
That no Muslim should be subject to have Christian soldiers billeted upon him or be transported to provinces of this kingdom against his will.
That both great and small should be perfectly secure in their persons, families and properties.
That they should be allowed to continue in their dwellings and residences, whether in the city, the suburbs or any other part of the country.
That no Christian should be allowed to peep over the wall or into the house of a Muslim or enter a mosque.
That any Muslim choosing to travel or reside among the Christians should be perfectly secure in his person and property.
That no Christian should enter the house of a Muslim or insult him in any way.
That no badge or distinctive mark be put upon them, as was done with the Jews and Mudejares.

That all Muslim captives taken during the siege of Granada, from whatever part of the country they might have come, but especially the nobles and chiefs mentioned in the agreement should be liberated.

That such Muslim captives as might have escaped from their Christian masters and taken refuge in Granada should not be surrendered, but the Sultan should be bound to pay the price of such captives to their owners.

That all those who might choose to cross over to Africa should be allowed to take their departure within a certain time and be conveyed thither in the king's ships, and without any pecuniary tax being imposed on them beyond the mere charge for passage, and that after the expiration of that time no Muslim should be hindered from departing provided he paid, in addition to the price of his passage, the tithe of whatever property he might carry along with him.

At the same time, Cardinal Francisco Jiménez de Cisneros, the archbishop of Toledo, arrived in Granada and began working alongside Talavera. Cisneros disliked Talavera's approach and began sending uncooperative Muslims, especially the noblemen, to prison, where they were treated harshly until they agreed to convert. Emboldened by the increase in conversions, Cisneros intensified the efforts, and on December 1499, he told Pope Alexander VI that three thousand Muslims converted in a single day. Cisneros's own church council warned that these methods might be a breach of the Treaty. The 16th-century hagiographer Álvar Gómez de Castro described the approach as "methods that were not correct".

In December 1499, amid the increasingly forced conversions and triggered by an incident involving an attempt by the authorities to reconvert a Muslim woman who had converted from Christianity, the population of Albayzín, the Muslim quarter of Granada, began an open and armed revolt. Talavera and Captain-General Tendilla resolved the situation by negotiating with the Muslims. Meanwhile, Cisneros was summoned to the court in Seville to account for his actions. He convinced the Catholic monarchs to issue a collective pardon to the rebels on the condition that they converted to Christianity. Consequently, the whole city of Granada nominally became Christian, and the treaty began to unravel.

Before 1492, Spain was a collection of diverse kingdoms with different laws and religions. The Treaty of Granada (and its subsequent violation) marked the moment Spain decided to become a unified nation-state with one religion (Catholicism) and one primary authority. This "Granada Model" where a state demands total cultural and religious uniformity from its citizens became the standard for European empires for the next several centuries.
The fall of Granada and the signing of the treaty were the final hurdles for the Spanish Crown's global ambitions.

articles.title: Mishima incident
paragraphs: The Mishima incident (三島事件, Mishima jiken) occurred on November 25, 1970, when the Japanese author Yukio Mishima committed seppuku (ritual suicide) after calling on the Japan Self-Defense Forces to stage a coup d'état to abolish Article 9 of the Japanese Constitution and appealing to his own ideas and beliefs about reconstructing true national autonomy. The incident is sometimes called the Tatenokai incident (楯の会事件, Tatenokai jiken), after the private militia led by Mishima whose members took part.

The incident shocked Japan and made international headlines because of such a renowned author's unprecedented actions. Mishima's death was seen to mark the end of an era. It also had a major impact on Japan's political climate, including the rise to the New Right, which grew out of minzoku-ha. A survey conducted by the monthly magazine Bungei Shunjū in 2000 on the "20 Greatest Events of the 20th Century," the Mishima Incident was ranked second, ahead of global events such as the fall of the Berlin Wall.

While the incident constituted a political protest meant to demonstrate their political vision, judicial investigations and Mishima's suicide notes reveal that the action itself was not intended to effect a government overthrow or a seizure of power. Even so, the incident is considered to possess significant historical importance and to have exerted a lasting impact on Japanese society.

Around 10:58 am on November 25, 1970, Yukio Mishima (age 45), along with four Tatenokai members – Masakatsu Morita (age 25), Masayoshi Koga (小賀正義; age 22), Masahiro Ogawa (小川正洋; age 22), and Hiroyasu Koga (age 23) – passed through the Yotsuya Gate (四谷門), the main gate of the Japan Ground Self-Defense Force Camp Ichigaya (市ヶ谷駐屯地) by car, arriving at the front entrance that led to the Commandant General's office on the second floor of the Eastern Army Headquarters. Guided by Major Yasuharu Sawamoto (沢本泰治), who met them there, they went up the front staircase, then escorted to the Commandant General’s office by Colonel Isamu Hara (原勇), Chief of the Administration Division of the Eastern Army HQ.

This visit had been booked in advance on November 21, and Sergeant Ryoichi Nakao (中尾良一) of the Operations Office had contacted the guard post via internal line to give them a free passage. The gatekeeper, Sergeant Akira Suzuki (鈴木偣), simply exchanged salutes with Mishima in the passenger seat and he was allowed through.

Led to the reception area and invited to take a seat, Mishima called out the names of Morita and the three others one by one – keeping them standing at attention – and introduced them to the Commander-in-Chief, Lieutenant General Kanetoshi Mashita (益田兼利; age 57), as "outstanding members" to be honored. He explained his reason for bringing the four along in the office, saying, "I brought these men today because during the trial enlistment in November, they selflessly carried an injured comrade on their backs all the way down the mountain. I will commend them at today's regular meeting at Ichigaya Hall (市ヶ谷会館), so I brought them here hoping to introduce them to you first. Since we have our meeting today, we came in formal uniform."

As General Mashita and Mishima were conversing on the sofa facing each other, the topic turned to the Japanese sword Mishima had brought with him. When Mashita asked, "Is it genuine?" and "Don't the police question you for carrying such a military sword (軍刀, guntō)?", Mishima replied, "This guntō (ceremonial sword) features a blade of Seki Magoroku (関孫六), remounted with military fittings. Would you like to see the certificate of authenticity?" and showed him the document inscribed with "Seki Kanemoto" (関兼元).

articles.title: NASA+ Content Coming to Big Screen at Greenbelt, Maryland Cinema
paragraphs: NASA announced Monday that NASA+ content has found its first theatrical home at The Greenbelt Cinema in Greenbelt, Maryland, expanding the agency’s reach across major viewing platforms and bringing space even closer to home.

“The National Aeronautics and Space Act of 1958 calls us to share our story of space exploration with the broadest possible audience, and our partners help us accomplish that,” said Rebecca Sirmons, general manager of NASA+ at the agency’s Headquarters in Washington. “Artemis II captured the imagination of the Artemis generation, but we are just getting started. With Artemis III on the horizon and our sights set on building humanity’s first Moon Base, this is only the beginning of our story being told, and we’ll continue sharing transparent, engaging content every step of the way.”

NASA and The Greenbelt Cinema will kick off their partnership with screenings of the NASA+ original documentary “The Europa Concept,” which follows NASA’s journey to investigate the science driving future exploration of Europa, Jupiter’s icy moon. Dates for screenings will be announced soon on NASA.gov.

Future programming may include other NASA+ original content, in-person live streaming events of NASA’s Artemis missions, including the first crewed mission to the Moon under the Artemis program, additional Europa content, and more. NASA+ also will remain available for free, with no ads, through the NASA app and on the agency’s website .

Earlier this year during its Ignition event, NASA outlined a bold path forward for the agency, including increasing the cadence of Artemis missions to the lunar surface, and building the first Moon Base, among other agency priorities. Partnerships like this one help NASA maximize engagement with communities around the world by making the agency’s missions and educational content available to viewers on their preferred devices and channels.
